en: Mahāyāna-vijñaptimātratā-śāstra, one fascicle.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
The path of cultivation is not shared with others; it can explain peerless meanings.
I prostrate to the principle of the Mahāyāna and shall now set forth its establishment and refutation.
Cultivated at the stations of immeasurable Buddhas, it removes both the obstacles and the root [of affliction].
The self-nature of consciousness-only is quiescent; those who are dull and inferior do not believe it.
Within the Mahāyāna, it is established that the three realms consist of nothing but consciousness, as the Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
The three realms consist of nothing but mind.
"Mind, thought, and consciousness" are general designations; one should know that this mind possesses associated mental factors (*citta-samprayukta-dharma*).
The word "only" (*kevala*) is used to exclude material objects (*rūpa-viṣaya*) and the like.
In reality, there are no external objects, for consciousness arises appearing as if there were objects;
it is just like a person with cataracts who sees hairs, two moons, and the like.
This is the tenet established in the Mahāyāna: that external objects do not exist at all.
If that is so, how is it that external objects are perceived?
To prove this point, it is said: "Because consciousness arises resembling an object.
Since consciousness manifests resembling an object, sentient beings perceive objects within the absence of objects.

To clarify this consciousness, this analogy is established: just as when the eye is diseased or the visual faculty is disturbed, consciousness manifests within the absence of any object as something resembling two moons, a mirage, or similar phenomena.
The meaning of Vijñapti-mātra is likewise: therefore, there are no external objects in the three realms; rather, consciousness transforms and manifests as if they were objects.
The three natures and the two truths are equally devoid of intrinsic nature, and this is termed the "non-established" (apratiṣṭhita).
If there were only consciousness and no external objects, then locations and times would have no fixed nature;
there would be no continuity and nothing would be fixed; and all purposeful activities would fail to be accomplished.
What meaning does this verse intend to reveal?

If consciousnesses such as that of form arise even when separated from the six sense objects, and do not arise from those objects, for what reason does this consciousness arise in certain locations and not in all locations?
Within these locations, why does it sometimes arise and sometimes not, rather than arising constantly?
If many people are together at the same time and in the same place, this consciousness arises as an indeterminate continuity rather than following any single individual.
It is like when a person with a cataract in the eye sees hairs or two moons, while others do not see them.
Furthermore, for what reason can the hair, flies, and other such objects perceived by one with cataracts not perform the functions of hair, flies, and so forth, while other objects can?
Likewise, why is it that the food, drink, clothing, poison, swords, staves, and so forth obtained in a dream cannot perform the functions of food, drink, and so forth, while other things can?
Furthermore, a city of the gandharvas is not actually existent and cannot perform the functions of a city, whereas other cities can.
If they are equally devoid of atoms, why do these four types of things differ?

Therefore, apart from external objects, these four factors—a fixed location, a fixed time, an unfixed continuity, and the performance of an action—would all be unestablished. Yet they are not unestablished;
rather, the meanings of fixed location and so forth are established, just as in a dream.
How is it that one is free from all sensory objects within a dream?
One may see countries, gardens, men, women, and so forth in certain places, but not in all places.
Or, even within those places, one sees them at some times and not at others, rather than seeing them constantly.
Therefore, when separated from sensory objects, the establishment of a fixed location and a fixed time is possible;
just as the continuity of hungry ghosts is indeterminate, so too can the indeterminate nature of their continuity be established.
How is this established?
It is because everyone perceives it equally as a river of pus.
Because pus completely fills the river, it is called a "river of pus," just like a jar filled with clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Because hungry ghosts share the same karmic retribution, they all see pus and other impurities filling the rivers; it is not just one person who sees them.
Just as they see rivers of pus, so too do they see rivers of excrement and other filth.
Or one may see someone holding a sword or staff to guard [the object], preventing others from approaching.
In this way, the continuity of consciousness-only is indeterminate; it can be established even in the absence of external objects, just as in a dream where one performs acts of killing.
Just as in a dream, the emission of semen occurs apart from the sexual union of a man and a woman, yet the dream-vision is established as a causal factor; so too is the performance of an action.
By means of this analogy, each of the four points—place, time, determination, and so forth—is established.
Furthermore, as in the case of the hells, all [the arguments] are established by means of the analogy of the hells through four points.
How are they established?
By seeing the hell-wardens and experiencing the shared infliction of harm.

Just as those people undergoing punishment in the hells see the hell-wardens and so forth, and at fixed places and times see dogs, crows, mountains, and the like coming—all of whom they see simultaneously, not one by one.

The same applies to the experience of being oppressed and harmed: although there are no actual wardens or the like, it occurs due to the predominant condition of shared karmic retribution; this is likewise true for other realms.
By means of this comprehensive analogy, the four points are established.
For what reason are the hell-wardens, dogs, crows, and so forth not admitted to be actual sentient beings?
Because it is illogical.
These wardens cannot be established as inhabitants of the hell realm who undergo punishment, for they cannot experience the sufferings of hell in the same manner as those who do.
If those beings in hell were to harm one another, how could one distinguish that "this is a hell-being" and "that is a warder"?
If their physical appearance and strength were identical, there would be no basis for the concept of mutual fear.
On the ground of red-hot iron, flames constantly arise; since they themselves cannot endure the suffering of being burned, how could they inflict harm upon others therein?
They are not denizens of hell; how, then, could they be born within hell?
How can animals be born in the heavens?
It is not the case that those distinct classes of beings such as hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts who are born within the hells are called "hell-wardens. This is not so.
Just as when animals are born in heaven, there is no intermediate state (antara-bhava) for those in hell;
because they cannot experience it, the retribution of suffering in hell does not occur.
If animals are born in heaven, through their mixed karma they are able to bring about the pleasure of the world, and within that birth, they receive the retribution of celestial bliss.
The hell-wardens and others are not like this, as they do not undergo the retribution of suffering in hell; therefore, it is illogical for animals or hungry ghosts to be born within the hells.
Due to the karma of sinners, beings resembling hell-wardens and the like are born.
If you grant that these [beings] are transformations, why do you not grant the same for consciousness?

Because of the karmic retribution of the denizens of hell, the four great elements manifest as various distinct categories, appearing with diverse forms, shapes, and dimensions; these are designated as "hell-wardens" and so forth.
The transformations are likewise; sometimes there appear the movements of hands and feet, which give rise to terror and perform acts of slaughter.

Or there are two mountains resembling rams that suddenly join and suddenly part; in the forest of iron trees, the sharp thorns of the iron trees are either lowered or raised. He says that such things are not non-existent.

Why is it not admitted that karma arises from consciousness and that consciousness itself undergoes transformation, rather than saying that these four great elements (mahābhūtas) undergo such transformation?
Furthermore:
"Karma perfumes consciousness within, while the grasping for results arises without."
For what reason is the fruit not mentioned within that locus of perfuming?
It is through the karma of these sinful persons that such things as the four great elements and their transformations can be seen within the hells.
This karmic perfuming resides within the continuum of consciousness of the hell-beings, not elsewhere.

This locus of perfuming is a transformation of consciousness appearing as hell-wardens and the like; it is the maturation of karma, yet you do not admit that it exists in its own location. Why then do you maintain such a position—that the fruit of karma arises in a place other than the locus of perfuming?
The Āgamas are the authority.

If consciousness were produced merely as resembling objects such as form while no external objects like form existed, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would not have taught that there truly exist the various bases (āyatana) such as form.
This Āgama is not a valid reason, for it does not represent the intended meaning of the Āgamas.

The inclusion of form and so forth [in the definition of the person] was taught according to a specific intention in order to transform those who cling to a self or a person, just as one speaks of "created beings" (nirmita).

As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has said that there are beings of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), he spoke of the uninterrupted continuity of illusion even unto future lives for the sake of a specific intention.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"There are no sentient beings and no self; there are only dharmas with their causes and effects."
Because it is explained separately in this manner, we know it is a distinct teaching.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke likewise regarding the various bases (āyatanas) such as form, in order to deliver those sentient beings who were suited to hear the teaching on the bases.
This explanation follows the intended meaning of the Teaching; what, then, is the distinct meaning?
Consciousness arises from its own seeds, manifesting and appearing as if they were external objects;
in order to establish the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*), the Buddha taught these two.
What meaning does this verse intend to reveal?

It shows that consciousness appearing as an object arises from a specific transformation of its own seeds; these seeds and the manifestation as the object serve as the gateway for the arising of consciousness appearing as form.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught in succession the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and the sense-base of forms (*rūpāyatana*), up to the consciousness resembling the cognition of touch (*spraṣṭavya-vijñāna*). From its own seed until the arising of a specific transformation, that seed and [the object] resembling touch manifest as the gateway for the means of generating the consciousness of touch; therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught them as the sense-base of the body (*kāyāyatana*) and the sense-base of touch (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
If one explains "entry" according to this meaning, what benefit is there?
If others rely on this teaching, they attain entry into the selflessness of persons;
through another teaching, they are able to eliminate conceptualization and enter the emptiness of phenomena.
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught the sense-bases (āyatana) based on this principle, his disciples to be converted would realize the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).
From the mere six pairs, only the six consciousnesses arise; there is not a single dharma that acts as a seer, nor even one that acts as a toucher.
If one understands this meaning as the teaching of the emptiness of persons, the disciples to be trained will enter into the emptiness of a personal self (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
By means of a distinct teaching—namely, the teaching of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)—they will enter into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
How does one enter into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)?
All phenomena arise as mere consciousness appearing as objects such as form; there is not a single phenomenon that possesses form or the like as its characteristic.
If one knows this, one enters into the emptiness of phenomena.
If all phenomena were entirely non-existent, then even this "consciousness-only" would not exist; how, then, could it be established?

It is not by asserting that all phenomena are entirely non-existent that one speaks of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*); nor is it by knowing this [literal] meaning that one is said to have entered into the emptiness of phenomena.
If that is so, how does one enter into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)?
One enters the emptiness of phenomena by eliminating the characteristics of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*).

Just as ordinary beings conceptually construct the characteristics of all phenomena, all phenomena are empty and non-existent by virtue of those very characteristics; this is called the emptiness of phenomena. It is not by means of an ineffable essence—the domain of the Buddhas—that the emptiness of phenomena is taught.
In this way, consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) is empty because its substance does not exist as it is discriminated by another consciousness.
If one enters into this principle, one establishes consciousness-only and enters into the emptiness of the self of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), without negating all phenomena as non-existent.

If it were not so, a distinct consciousness would have to take a distinct object as its domain, and the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) would fail to be established, because the objects of consciousness would exist substantially.
How can this be believed?

Based on this meaning, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught that the sense-bases such as form exist; however, this is not because there are substantially real sense-bases such as form that serve as the objects of visual consciousness and the other cognitions.
It is by virtue of this principle that this meaning is to be trusted.
External objects and atoms are neither identical nor different;
those aggregates are not objects either, because atoms are not established.
What meaning does this verse intend to reveal?

Are these bases, such as visible form, each the respective object of visual consciousness and so forth, as a single unit with its atoms— as the Vaiśeṣikas maintain regarding "composite matter" (avayavi-rūpa)—
or are they not a single unit, because the atoms are distinct?
Is it that this aggregate of atoms (*paramāṇu*) as a form-base (*rūpāyatana*) constitutes a single object of visual consciousness together with those atoms?
This interpretation is not correct.

For a whole (*sāvayava-rūpa*) cannot be perceived as a distinct entity within its parts; nor can many atoms be perceived individually; nor can they be perceived as an accumulated mass (*rajas*), because atoms do not constitute a single substance.
How is it that [the atom] cannot be established?
When six [atoms] come together at once, the atom would have six sides.
If the six were in the same location, the aggregate would be the size of a single atom.
Suppose six atoms come from six directions and assemble together with a single atom.
This single atom does not constitute a single entity, because it possesses six directional parts.
This is because another atom cannot occupy the same location as one atom.

If the location of one atom were identical to the locations of six atoms, then all things would occupy the same single location; consequently, all composite objects would have the same magnitude as a single atom, as they could not mutually exceed one another in size.
If it were the size of an atom, even an aggregate would not be visible.
If you say that atoms cannot aggregate because they lack spatial parts, then this fault does not arise.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr maintain that these atoms (paramāṇu) within an aggregate are mutually associated; this being their position, they should be questioned as follows:
regarding the objects you describe as atomic aggregates, these aggregates are not distinct from the atoms themselves.
If atoms do not join together, what within the aggregate could be in conjunction?
Furthermore, if they lack spatial parts, an aggregate of atoms cannot be established.
If atoms have no conjunction, to what phenomenon within the aggregate does this conjunction belong?
If you say that atoms can mutually combine with one another,
this is not the case. Why is that?
Since atoms have no spatial parts,
if their aggregation cannot be established, how much less can there be a conventionally designated collection?
It should be stated thus.
Since an aggregate possesses spatial dimensions, if the meaning of "conjunction" cannot be established for it, how could atoms that lack spatial dimensions possibly achieve conjunction?
Therefore, an atom is not established as a single entity.
Whether the aggregation of atoms can burn or cannot burn is not discussed here.
If a thing possesses spatial divisions, it should not constitute a single entity.
The eastern part of an atom is distinct from its parts in the other five directions, and the same applies down to its lower part.
If these parts are distinct, and if the atom takes these parts as its substance, how can it be established as a single entity?
Furthermore, what is the nature of shadow and obstruction?
If a single atom (*paramāṇu*) has no spatial divisions, how can there be a shadow on one side when the sun is rising?
Why is this question asked?
In these atoms, there is no distinct part that is directly illuminated by the sun.
Furthermore, if these atoms and those atoms were both devoid of spatial parts, how could they obstruct one another?
Why is this? Because these atoms (*paramāṇu*) have no further parts by which they could join with others such that their arrival would constitute an obstruction.

If there were no obstruction, then because all atoms of the six directions would occupy the same location, every aggregate would be the same size as a single atom; this point has already been explained previously.
These shadows and obstructions belong to the aggregate (saṃghāta) and not to the atoms (paramāṇu); why do you not accept this principle?
Do you now admit that the aggregate is something distinct from the atoms?
Is it for this reason that you say shadows and obstructions belong to the aggregate? No.
If they were identical, there would be no duality; if they were aggregated, they would not differ from atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Therefore, this shadow and this obstruction do not belong to the aggregate. Why is this so?
It is merely the conceptual differentiation of forms and appearances that we call an "aggregate"; why then engage in such deliberation?
Since the essential characteristics of the objects of the senses, such as form and so forth, have not yet been dismantled, what could possibly constitute their essence?
The objects of the eyes and other senses, as well as categories such as blue and so forth—this matter should be considered together.

Regarding these objects of the eyes and other senses, as well as categories such as blue and so forth, which you maintain to be the substance of the sense-field (*viṣaya*): are they many things, or are they a single thing?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If there were many, the fault would be as previously stated;
if there were only one, there would likewise be an error.
As a verse says:
If there were no single [entity] proceeding in succession, There would be no simultaneity, nor what has been attained or not yet attained,
Nor distinct categories, nor manifold things, Nor even the subtle that is difficult to perceive.
If all [colors] such as blue and yellow were without distinction and the eye’s object were apprehended as a single entity, then there would be no sequential movement upon the ground.
If one were to set down a foot once, it should traverse the entirety of it at once.
That which has already been obtained here and that which has not yet been obtained there cannot both exist simultaneously.

Why? Because within a single moment, a single entity cannot possess both the states of having been obtained and not yet having been obtained; nor can it possess multiple distinct categories, such as an army consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth, nor can it possess multiple distinct entities.
Why is this? Since many things are contained within the locus of a single thing, how could the distinction between "this" and "that" be established?
Furthermore, what constitutes "one," such that the space between these two reaches is empty?
Furthermore, this most minute water-insect is of the same color as the large one; there is no sense in which it cannot be seen.
If you maintain that there is a distinct entity based on the distinction of characteristics such as color and other objects, rather than by way of some other principle.
If that were so, one would have to distinguish the differences among objects by means of distinct types of atoms; in that case, atoms could not constitute a single entity.
Since the five objects, such as form and the rest, are not the actual domains of the eye and the other senses, the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) is thereby established.

Regarding "all objects" (*dharmas*): they have consciousness and the factors associated with consciousness as their essence. Because they are free from the grasper and the grasped, they do not increase; because they establish correct cause and effect, they do not decrease. They are devoid of uncausedness and unequal causes; the two kinds of emptiness and the twelvefold dependent origination constitute their very nature.
As a verse says:

"Whether something exists or does not exist can be determined as right or wrong by relying on the various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); among all such means, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the most excellent.
If external objects were truly non-existent, how could such perceptual cognition arise?"
What is called "I have realized this" is a realization of wisdom that is like a dream. Just as when one dreams,
one perceives forms such as mountains and trees while being devoid of external objects, so too there are no external objects.
The realized wisdom is also like this:
at the time of realized wisdom, no object is seen;
how then can an object be realized?
As you have said, when realized wisdom arises, one thinks, "I have realized this.

At that time, you cannot perceive the external object; it is merely a conceptualization of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), for the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) has already ceased. How, then, can that object be realized?
If one asserts that things perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇabhanga*), then at that time, for such a person, form (*rūpa*) up to touch (*spraṣṭavya*) have already ceased.
Question:

If something is not cognized by the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), the mental consciousness (*manas*) cannot retain it as a memory; therefore, the five sense objects (*pañcaviṣaya*) are necessarily cognized by the five consciousnesses.
"Valid cognition (pramāṇa) is what is called 'seeing'; therefore, the six objects such as form are said to be the objects of realization.
Answer:
This interpretation is not correct; for one first realizes the object and only subsequently maintains it through recollection.
Why is this? As it is said regarding consciousness appearing as objects:
apart from the six objects such as form, the six consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, arise appearing as those six objects.
This meaning is as previously explained.
From this, recollection arises.

From this, there exists a consciousness resembling the object; the conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), associated with recollection, arises at a later time resembling the object that was previously produced. Therefore, one must not maintain that [the mental consciousness] arises solely from recollection, asserting that it first perceives the object through consciousness.
If, as in a dream, consciousness can arise even in the absence of external objects,

then just as people know for themselves during the waking state that dream-consciousness lacks external objects, they should likewise know for themselves that waking-consciousness lacks external objects.
Since this is not the case, we know that the objects perceived during the waking state differ from those perceived in a dream.
Furthermore, while dreams have the characteristic of arising again [as memories], the waking state does not; therefore, it is not the case that there are no objects at all in the waking state.
Answer:
This statement does not constitute proof.
One sees objects in a dream though they do not exist; yet, while one has not yet awakened, one cannot know this.

Thus, through the habitual cultivation of such false conceptualization until it has become thoroughly matured, worldly people perceive unreal objects as if they were real, just like what is seen in a dream;
yet upon awakening, it is not so, for one can then correctly understand that the objects of the dream do not exist.

Thus, when a practitioner cultivates the supramundane path of remedy and attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), entering the stage of seeing the unestablished noble truths (*anabhilapya-āryasatya*) and attaining awakening—at that time, both non-conceptual wisdom and the subsequently attained pure mundane wisdom perceive the six sense objects as they truly are: as having no existence whatsoever. This meaning is equal [in both].

If it is because of the transformation and excellence within one's own continuum that the six consciousnesses of sentient beings arise resembling the six objects—rather than actually arising from those objects—then by associating with virtuous or non-virtuous friends and hearing the two types of teachings, the correct and the false, sentient beings come to possess the two states of meditative concentration: the correct and the false.
How is this established?
If that which is closely associated and that which is spoken of are both non-existent,
then because they mutually act as dominant conditions, the two consciousnesses are determined as either correct or erroneous.
Because all sentient beings arise through the predominance of mutual consciousness, two kinds of consciousness are necessarily established: either right determination or wrong determination.
"Mutual" means that self and others together accomplish the affairs of both self and others.

Therefore, because of the superior capacity of the distinct continuity of consciousness, it arises from the superior capacity of that distinct continuity of consciousness, and not from external objects.

If waking consciousness were like dream-consciousness in having no objective realm, why would the two results of love and hatred, or good and evil deeds performed by a person in both the dreaming and waking states, be different in the future?
The dream-consciousness is impaired by sleep, and thus its future fruit differs [from waking consciousness].
This is the correct reason why the dreaming mind lacks karmic retribution: because it is impaired by torpor and sleep, the mind is too weak to accomplish wholesome or unwholesome karma.
Question:
If all things are merely consciousness, then there would be no body or speech.
How is it that domestic animals such as oxen and sheep die from being slaughtered by butchers?
If that death were not caused by the butcher, how could the butcher incur the sin of killing?
The answer is:
Through the transformation of another's consciousness, the event of death is accomplished here.
As in the case of others losing their minds and so forth, it is due to the power of the mind of a spirit or similar being.

Just as through the transformation of the mind of a spirit, ghost, or the like, various transformations are brought about, such that another person may lose mindfulness, experience dreams, or become possessed by spirits and the like.
Furthermore, due to the mental resolve of those possessing supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such things occur.
For example, King Śarabha and others obtained dreams through the mental resolve of Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, because of the wrathful mind of an araṇya seer, King Vemacitrin perceives a terrifying sight.
In this way, through the transformation of another's consciousness, one is able to sever the life-faculty of another.
For this reason, the cessation of the continuity of a similar type is called "death"; this meaning should be understood.
Furthermore:
Why is it that the Tāṇḍa forest became empty and desolate due to the anger of the ṛṣi?

If one does not admit that the death of sentient beings occurs due to the predominant transformation of another's consciousness, then how would the Blessed One establish that mental transgression (*cetanā*) is the greatest of sins? He asked the householder Upāli:
"Householder!"
"Have you ever heard how the Tāṇḍaka grove, the Karaṅka grove, and the Mātaṅga grove are empty, tranquil, and pure?
The householder replied:
Gautama! We have heard that due to the resentment of a seer, a heavy mental punishment results in a great sin; if this is so, how can [the path] be accomplished?
If you maintain that various spirits and deities, out of affection and respect for the rishis, kill the sentient beings therein, rather than the rishis acting out of a mind of hatred,
then why is it that the mental karma resulting from this constitutes a heavy punishment and a grave offense more severe than a heavy punishment of body or speech?
Because of the ṛṣi’s mind of anger, many sentient beings died; thus, the gravity of his mental retribution constitutes a great sin.
If all things are merely consciousness, does one who possesses the supernormal power of knowing others' minds know the minds of others, or not?
If that is so, what is the reason?
If one does not know [the object], how can one attain the supernormal power of knowing others' minds?
If one does know it, why say that consciousness has no external object?
The wisdom of one possessing the supernormal power of knowing others' minds—how could it not be like its object?
Since it knows its own mind, why does it not know [the minds of others] as they are, like the domain of a Buddha?
If this is the domain of the knowledge of others' minds, how could it not be like [that domain]?
Due to a lack of wisdom, the mind of another is established as having an ineffable nature; such is the domain of the Buddha, which cannot be known [by others].
These two domains are not equal, because they do not appear in that way, and because the conceptualization of grasper and grasped has not been extinguished.
This principle of consciousness-only is inexhaustible; its analytical categories are profoundly deep and bottomless.

Having established the principle of consciousness-only, I have composed this according to my own ability, in accordance with the principle and the measure, regarding the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas and others.
We have exerted every effort, yet we cannot conceive or fathom this principle, for this principle is not an object of discursive thought (*vitarka*) or investigation (*vicāra*).
Who is capable of fully penetrating this realm?
This is the realm of the Buddhas. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess unimpeded knowledge regarding all phenomena; according to their measure and according to the principle, this realm is seen only by the Buddhas.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu is hereby completed.
Previously, Dharma Master Bodhiruci had translated the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* at the Northern Court.

On the sixteenth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Tiānjiā era of the Chen dynasty, in the year of Kǒuwèi, Huìkǎi invited the Tripiṭaka Master Kuṇāla at Zhìzhǐ Temple in Guǎngzhōu to retranslate this treatise; he translated it while lecturing on it, completing the work on the fifth day of the third month.
This treatise originally possessed a commentary in a foreign edition, which was translated into two fascicles.
The Tripiṭaka Master further explained the original text, and Huikai recorded these notes, resulting in another two fascicles.

Later, there was the Dharma Master Shi Ren, who brought an old manuscript from Jin’an to Fanyu. Seng Kai took the new text and collated it against the old one; while the general meaning remained largely the same, the verses differed.
Furthermore, the prose explanations were verbose yet deficient in meaning, and the treatise lacked an initial expression of homage.
Discerning gentlemen should investigate this thoroughly.
I now respectfully transcribe the verses separately and place them after the treatise, so that those who peruse it may find it easier to read.
This treatise represents the correct doctrine of the Buddha-dharma and is widely propagated in foreign lands.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Huikai:
Cultivating the path not in common with others, Able to expound peerless meanings—
I prostrate to the principle of the Mahāyāna, And shall now set forth its establishment and refutation.
Cultivated at the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas, It removes both obstacles and their roots;
The self-nature of consciousness is quiescent, Yet those who are dull and inferior do not delight in it.
In reality, no external objects exist, For consciousness arises appearing as if they were objects.
Just as a person with cataracts Sees hairs, two moons, and the like;
Place and time are entirely without fixity, There is no continuity and nothing is fixed,
And all purposeful action is unaccomplished, If there were only consciousness and no external objects.
The establishment of objects such as those in meditative concentration is like a dream or like [the vision of] hungry ghosts;
all things are indeterminate in their continuity, just as many see the river of pus together.
Like the performance of deeds in a dream that cause harm, and furthermore, like [the experiences in] the hells.
They see all the hell-wardens and suffer their persecutions together; yet,
like animals born in heaven, they do not experience the intermediate state within the hells,
for they cannot undergo the retributive suffering therein.
Due to the karma of sinners, beings resembling hell-wardens and the like arise;
if you grant that those [beings] are transformations [of consciousness], why do you not grant this for them?
Since the karmic latencies are within consciousness, yet you insist that the fruit arises externally.
For what reason is the fruit not mentioned within the locus of perfuming?
Because the sense-bases such as form are taught for the sake of transforming those who cling to a self or a person;
they are spoken according to a specific intention, just as one speaks of "born from transformation."
Consciousness arises from its own seeds, manifesting as if it were external objects;
in order to establish the internal and external sense bases, the Buddha taught these two.
If others rely upon this teaching, they will attain entry into the selflessness of persons.
Through the specific teaching, one can eliminate [the view of self] and enter the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
External objects and atoms (*paramāṇu*) are neither identical nor different;
that aggregate is not an object either, because atoms are not established.
When six [atoms] come together at once, the atom would have six sides;
if the six were in the same location, the aggregate's size would be that of a single atom.
If atoms do not join, what within the aggregate could be in conjunction?
Furthermore, if there were no spatial parts, an aggregate of atoms could not be established.
If an object possessed spatial parts, it could not be a single entity;
how then could shadow and obstruction occur?
If they were identical, there would be no duality.

If they were one, there would be no sequential activity; there would be no distinction between what has already been attained and what has not yet been attained, nor would there be various distinct categories or manifold phenomena, nor would there be subtle things difficult to perceive.
Just as with realized wisdom in a dream, at that time one is like realized wisdom;
at that time no object is seen—how then can an object be realized?
As it is said, consciousness appears as an object, and from this, recollection arises.
Seeing that dust is non-existent in a dream, one cannot know it so long as one has not awakened.
Because they mutually influence one another, the two consciousnesses are determined as either correct or erroneous.
Dream-consciousness is impaired by sleep; thus, the future fruits are not the same.
Through the transformation of another’s consciousness, the event of death occurs here,
just as others lose their minds due to the mental power of spirits and the like.
How is it that the Tāṇḍava forest became empty and desolate through the anger of a seer?
If the mind punishes great offenses with heavy penalties, how could such a thing be possible?
The wisdom of one possessing the supernormal power of knowing others' minds is not like its object;
why is this so? Because it knows its own mind, it does not know [others'] as the Buddha’s object does.
Having accomplished the principle of Consciousness-Only, I have composed this treatise according to my own ability;
it accords with the principles and the measure of reality—the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas and others.
*Treatise on Mahāyāna Consciousness-Only* (Mahāyānavijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra)
